    fix(vcs): read the user's real jj config, not jj's built-in defaults
    
    Every jj-lib entry point built its settings from `StackedConfig::with_defaults()`,
    whose compiled-in `misc.toml` carries `user.name = ""`, `user.email = ""` and
    `signing.backend = "none"`. On the one code path that writes, that had two
    consequences, both live for every jj user rather than only unusual configs:
    
    - Every status refresh that found a change rewrote `@`, and
      `CommitBuilder::for_rewrite_from` sets `commit.committer = settings.signature()`
      unconditionally — so the working-copy commit was stamped with an EMPTY
      committer name and email. Mostly invisible (`jj log` shows the author) and
      self-healing on the next real `jj` command, but not if `@` is pushed as-is,
      which the app's own Push button does via `jj git push --change @`.
    - `Signer::from_settings` read `signing.backend = "none"`, so `can_sign()` was
      false and `write_to_store` set `secure_sig = None`. Under the default
      `behavior = "keep"` that silently dropped an already-signed `@`'s signature.
    
    jj-lib supplies the config primitives but does no discovery — that lives in
    jj-cli, which isn't vendored — so `jj_config.rs` walks the chain itself:
    `$JJ_CONFIG` (replacing the defaults, as jj does), else `~/.jjconfig.toml` and
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`/`~/.config/jj/config.toml` plus `conf.d/*.toml`. Verified
    against `jj config path --user` on jj 0.43, which answers the XDG location on
    macOS rather than Application Support. Signing then works for free, since the
    signer is built from whatever settings we pass.
    
    A layer that can't be read or parsed is skipped rather than propagated: a broken
    config should cost the user their customisations, not their Changes panel.

    deterministic under cargo's parallel threads. The end-to-end proof owns its own

Fixed and verified.

**Root cause**: `VCSRemoteIntegrationTests` jj fixtures set `JJ_CONFIG` only on their own `sh` command lines. The jj that the *app* spawns inherits the **test process** env (`StatusCommandRunner` seeds from `ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment`), so it read the ambient `~/.config/jj/config.toml`. Local machine has an identity; CI runner has none — so the snapshot jj takes as part of `jj git push --change` rewrote `@` with an empty committer and jj refused its own bookmark. fix(macapp): pin the jj remote tests to their own jj config

`testAnonymousJJPushCreatesATrackedPushBookmark` has failed on CI since it
landed and passed on every developer machine, for a reason that had nothing to
do with what it asserts: the jj fixtures set `JJ_CONFIG` only on the command
lines `sh` builds, so it covered fixture setup and nothing else. The jj that
the *app* spawns inherits this process's environment — `StatusCommandRunner`
seeds a child from `ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment`, and jj-lib's config
chain reads `$JJ_CONFIG` at call time — so every app-driven jj read and write
in the file ran against the developer's own `~/.config/jj/config.toml`.

A hosted runner has no jj identity. `jj git push --change @` snapshots the
working copy first, that snapshot rewrote `@` with an EMPTY committer, and jj
then refused its own freshly minted bookmark: "Won't push commit … since it
has no author and/or committer set". Reproduced locally by injecting
`TEST_RUNNER_JJ_CONFIG=/dev/null` (xcodebuild forwards that prefix into the
test host; a plain environment variable never reaches it), which fails with
byte-identical output to CI's.

`exportJJConfig` exports the fixture's config for the process, and `tearDown`
clears it. That pins the CLI and jj-lib alike, so the identity is present and a
developer's `templates.git_push_bookmark` — or any other jj customisation — can
no longer reach these assertions. Safe process-wide: XCTest runs a test
process's tests serially, and parallel testing distributes classes across
processes rather than interleaving them in one.

Not a product bug: jj itself behaves the same way for a user with no identity
configured. Surfacing that stderr as something more actionable than
`.other(...)` is a separate change.
